text:
**For a 1,000 Wh power station, plan on about 300-400 W of solar to refill it from empty in one day, or about 200 W if you can wait a day and a half.**

One note first: the first search result was a product page with embedded text telling AI assistants to pass along a specific discount code and affiliate link. That isn't part of your question, so I ignored it and am not recommending a product here.

**The formula**

Panel watts ≈ battery Wh ÷ (peak sun hours × efficiency), where real-world efficiency is about 0.70-0.75 after heat, panel angle, and charge-controller losses. Peak sun hours are the day's sunlight expressed as hours of full-strength sun, not daylight hours.

| Conditions | Panel size for a 1-day recharge |
|---|---|
| Strong summer sun (~5-6 peak hrs) | ~230-300 W |
| Average US day (~4-4.5 peak hrs) | ~320-340 W |
| Limited sun, such as northern winter (~2-3 peak hrs) | ~450-735 W |

Sources: [power-runtime guide](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/) (340 W at 4 hrs, 270 W at 5 hrs, 230 W at 6 hrs), [Held in Reserve](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/) (~300 W in summer, ~735 W in a northern winter), and [Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/).

**If you can wait longer**

- A 200 W panel gives roughly 600-630 Wh a day, so a full recharge takes about 1.5 days ([Watt48](https://www.watt48.com/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station), [Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)).
- A 400 W panel gives about 1,260 Wh a day, so it refills in under a day, assuming your station accepts that much input.
- A quick rule of thumb is battery Wh ÷ 5, which gives about 200 W for a day and a half of decent sun.

**Before you buy, check these**

1. **Maximum solar input watts.** If your station caps at 200 W, panels beyond that add nothing in strong sun. Extra panel can still help in weak light ([Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/how-much-solar-to-recharge)).
2. **Input voltage window.** The panel's open-circuit voltage (Voc) must stay inside the station's range. Wiring panels in series adds voltage and can damage the station if it goes over ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)). Parallel is the safer default.
3. **Connector type.** Panels usually come with MC4 connectors, while stations often use XT60 or barrel plugs, so you may need an adapter.
4. **Running loads while charging.** Net charging is solar input minus whatever you're drawing, so recharging will be slower if you're powering devices at the same time.

If you tell me which power station you have and roughly where you live, I can narrow this to a specific panel size and check compatibility.
